props.title: Hagazussa

sections.content: **Hagazussa (2017)** (2017) marks a stunning debut from Lukas Feigelfeld, diving deep into folk horror's darkest corners with a visual style reminiscent of The Witch (2015). Set in 15th century Alps, it shares DNA with Viy (1967) and **Valerie and Her Week of Wonders** (1970) in its exploration of pagan mysticism and female persecution. The film's hypnotic pacing and minimal dialogue create an atmosphere of creeping dread that recalls **Vampyr** (1932) while pushing folk horror into bold new territory.

sections.content: What sets **Hagazussa** (2017) apart is its unflinching look at isolation and madness. Like **Antichrist** (2009) and **The Devil's Backbone** (2001), it uses supernatural elements to explore deeper psychological trauma. The film's four-chapter structure mirrors the seasons, drawing parallels to pagan traditions seen in **The Wicker Man** (1973) while maintaining a distinctly Central European perspective on folklore and witchcraft.

The cinematography by Mariel Baqueiro deserves special attention, creating compositions that echo Bergman's **Hour of the Wolf** (1968) and Tarkovsky's **Mirror** (1975). Each frame is meticulously crafted to emphasize the protagonist's isolation against harsh Alpine landscapes, similar to the visual approach in **The Dark and the Wicked** (2020). sections.content: **Hagazussa** (2017) sits at the forefront of contemporary folk horror revival alongside **Midsommar** (2019) and **The Ritual** (2017). These films share a common thread of exploring ancient practices through a modern lens, while maintaining connections to classics like **Blood on Satan's Claw** (1971) and **Witchfinder General** (1968).
